214	\subsection{Multiplication, Division, Modulo, and Remainder Operators}
215	
216	For most integer, rational, floating-point, complex, and interval expressions,
217	multiplication can be expressed using any of `\EXP{\cdot}' or
218	`\EXP{\times}' or simply juxtaposition.
219	However,
220	the \EXP{\times} operator is used to
221	express the shape of matrices, so if expressions using multiplication are used
222	in expressing the shape of a matrix, it may be necessary to avoid the
223	use of '\EXP{\times}' to
224	express multiplication, or to use parentheses.
225	
226	For integer, rational, floating-point, complex, and interval expressions, division is expressed by \EXP{/}.
227	When the operator \EXP{/} is used to divide one integer by another,
228	the result is rational.
229	The operator \EXP{\div} performs truncating integer division:
230	\EXP{m \div n = \mathit{signum}\left({m \over n}\right) \left\lfloor \left| {m \over n} \right| \right\rfloor}.
231	The operator \OPR{REM} gives the remainder from such a truncating division:
232	\EXP{m \OPR{REM} n = m - n (m \div n)}.
233	The operator \OPR{MOD} gives the remainder from a floor division:
234	\EXP{m \OPR{MOD} n = m - n \left\lfloor {m \over n} \right\rfloor};
235	when \EXP{n>0} this is the usual modulus computation that evaluates integer \VAR{m}
236	to an integer \VAR{k} such that \EXP{0\leq{}k<n} and \VAR{n} evenly divides \EXP{m-k}.
237	
238	The special operators \OPR{DIVREM} and \OPR{DIVMOD} each return a pair of values,
239	the quotient and the remainder; \EXP{m \OPR{DIVREM} n} returns
240	\EXP{(m \div n, m \OPR{REM} n)} while
241	\EXP{m \OPR{DIVMOD} n} returns
242	\EXP{(\left\lfloor {m \over n} \right\rfloor, m \OPR{MOD} n)}.
243	
244	Multiplication of a vector or matrix by a scalar is done with juxtaposition,
245	as is multiplication of a vector by a matrix (on either side).  Vector dot product
246	is expressed by `\EXP{\cdot}' and vector cross product by
247	`\EXP{\times}'.  Division of
248	a matrix or vector by a scalar may be expressed using `\EXP{/}'.
249	
250	The syntactic interaction of juxtaposition, \EXP{\cdot}, \EXP{\times},
251	and \EXP{/} is subtle.
252	\See{operator-precedence} for a discussion of the relative precedence of
253	these operations and how precedence may depend on the use of whitespace.
254	
255	The handling of overflow depends on the type of the number produced.
256	For integer results, overflow throws an \TYP{IntegerOverflow}.
257	Rational computations do not overflow.
258	For floating-point results, overflow produces \EXP{+\infty} or \EXP{-\infty}
259	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
260	For intervals, overflow produces an appropriate containing interval.
261	
262	Underflow is relevant only to floating-point computations and is handled
263	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
264	
265	The handling of division by zero depends on the type of the number produced.
266	For integer results, division by zero throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero}.
267	For rational results, division by zero produces \EXP{1/0}.
268	For floating-point results, division by zero produces a \TYP{NaN} value
269	according to the rules of IEEE 754.
270	For intervals, division by zero produces an appropriate containing interval
271	(which under many circumstances will be the interval of all possible real values and infinities).
272	
273	Wraparound multiplication on fixed-size integers is expressed by
274	\EXP{\dottimes}.
275	Saturating multiplication on fixed-size integers is expressed by
276	\EXP{\boxdot} or \EXP{\boxtimes}.
277	These operations do not overflow.
278	
279	Ordinary multiplication and division of floating-point numbers always
280	use the IEEE 754 ``round to nearest'' rounding mode.  This rounding
281	mode may be emphasized by using the operators \EXP{\otimes} (or \EXP{\odot})
282	and \EXP{\oslash}.  Multiplication and division in ``round toward zero''
283	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\boxtimes} (or \EXP{\boxdot}) and
284	\EXP{\boxslash}.
285	Multiplication and division in ``round toward positive infinity''
286	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\uptimes} (or \EXP{\updot}) and \EXP{\upslash}.
287	Multiplication and division in ``round toward negative infinity''
288	mode may be expressed with \EXP{\downtimes} (or \EXP{\downdot}) and
289	\EXP{\downslash}.

content.content:
## The disk allowance

`df -h /` misleads. Its Size column is the whole disk, about 250 GB, and most of it is reserved and cannot be written. The session may use Used plus Avail, about 37 GB, and Use% is taken of that sum. Read the Avail column: it is what is left.

- When the allowance is full, tool output fails with "no space left on device". Check Avail before a long run, and before you seed worktrees or copy builds.
- Temporary files that the work never deletes fill it. In this repository, they are mostly the parser's folders in `/tmp`. `fortress-repo`'s `references/build-and-caches.md` gives their sweep.
- When it is full, stop your own background processes (`fortress-repo`'s `references/session.md`). Delete what you made and no longer need: scratch, build output, private caches, and finished worktrees whose commits are pushed.
- If that is not enough, commit and push, and report that this session's allowance is spent. A new session starts on a fresh machine.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.
add, rewrite, close and duplicate check the whole line they write; note checks
only what it changes (the notes cell and the row's length), so that a row
failing the template elsewhere still takes a note. A row at its length limit
takes no note: rewrite cuts it back (the rework's decision D4, "each is cut
when next edited", process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md).

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
  add FILE --section TITLE   FILE holds one row line, its # cell `?` (or the
                             seven cells after it); numbers it max + 1 and
                             inserts it in that section's table in number
                             order
  note N TEXT                adds TEXT to row N's notes, before the row's own
                             "full text: history, row N" marker where it has
                             one, else at their end (notes of `none` are
                             replaced); checks the notes cell and the row's
                             length only, so a failure in another cell does
                             not block it; a row keeps its own cells
  rewrite N FILE             FILE holds row N's whole new line (its # cell N
                             or ?, or the seven cells after it); checks it
                             against the template and writes it in the row's
                             place, its earlier line in the history
                             ("rewritten"): the route that corrects a claim,
                             cuts notes, or moves a reproducer. A FIXED or
                             DUPLICATE row stays so (a FIXED row's commit is
                             checked); a row becomes one only by close or
                             duplicate
  close N --commit HASH --test NAME [--settled TEXT] [--note TEXT] [--claim C]

\subsection{The interpreter's choice of a coercion}
\seclabel{revival-coercion-walk}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{resolving-coercion}.
\item[Change] One box after the example of the paragraph that says that
coercion is resolved statically; the paragraph and its example are unchanged.
The box says that the compiled path follows the text; that the interpreter,
which has no static types, chooses a coercion on the value and so runs
\EXP{f(B)} for the example's \EXP{f(c)}, and answers the same way wherever an
argument's value is of a type that another declaration already fits; that both
cases are gated as expected failures; and that the interpreter is to follow the
text once it takes the coercions that the compiled type checker inserts.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that the interpreter's choice of a coercion on the value is
its limit, since it has no static types from which to resolve a coercion
statically, and that the interpreter is made to follow the text once the
compiled type checker checks the programs it runs and it takes the coercions the
checker inserts.
The type group's paper of 2019 also carries the static types of calls to run
time for its dispatcher, which the interpreter does not have.
\item[Effect] None on the language.
The interpreter's answer, 4 where the text gives 3, and its answer in the
narrower case are gated by
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXCoercionStaticRungC.fss} and

\begin{quote}
Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is statically

\subsection{An abstract method of an exported trait}
\seclabel{revival-export-abstract}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{export-statements}.
\item[Change] The rule by which a trait or object declaration of a component
satisfies an exported one asks, beside a satisfying declaration for each field
declaration and non-abstract method declaration of the exported declaration, a
method declaration for each abstract method declaration of it, with the same
header apart from the modifier \KWD{abstract}, with a body or without one.
The sentence that allows a concrete declaration for an abstract method stands.
The passage gains a box.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows the
revival's decision of 25~October 2026, which the revival confirmed against this
passage on 29~October 2026, that a method that an \apiN\ declares abstract is
declared in the component that exports the \apiN.
The decision takes the type group's later work over this text, as the revival
does wherever the two conflict.
The compiler's own library declares, in its \apiN, the abstract methods of its
trait \TYP{GeneratorZZ32}, such as \VAR{loop}, and restates each of them in its
component without a body
(\nolinkurl{Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi}, lines 110--120, and
\nolinkurl{Library/CompilerLibrary.fss}, lines 301--312, in the revival's
repository).
The team's compiled type checker compared every member of an exported trait
with the component's: in 2009 member by member, an abstract method matched
by a declaration of the same header apart from the modifier \KWD{abstract}
(Sukyoung Ryu, commit \texttt{edb516dba}), and in its snapshots of 2011 and
2012 by refusing a component whose trait has fewer members than the
exported one (commit \texttt{5a68404fd}, the last).
The code generator makes a call of a method through a trait an interface call
on the component's declaration of the trait, so a compiled call of an abstract
method that the component's trait leaves out, or declares at another header,
stops at run time with \texttt{NoSuchMethodError}, also where every object
defines the method (row~816 of the revival's gap ledger).
\Library\ followed the earlier practice of the interpreter, which finds a
method on the object by name at a call and never needed the declaration, and
left twelve such methods undeclared in their component
\TYP{FortressLibrary}; the component now declares them, without bodies.
The text of \secref{apis}, which asks a matching definition to include
definitions for all declarations other than the methods and fields declared
abstract, is unchanged: it asks no body for an abstract method, and the revised
rule asks none either.
A reversal would restore the original sentences and return the compiled
export check to asking no declaration for an abstract method of an exported
trait, so that a compiled call of a method that a component leaves out stops
at run time again; the twelve declarations of \library\ would then be
unnecessary, though harmless, or the code generator would declare such a
method in the component's interface itself, a change that still leaves a
method declared at another header, a narrower return type and a functional
method failing at run time.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-abstract-declared/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker refuses a component whose trait leaves
out a method that the exported trait declares abstract (``missing members of
the trait/object in the component'') or declares it at another header
(``different method''), and takes a declaration with a body or without one.
The interpreter compares no component with the \apisN\ it exports, so it loads
and runs a component that leaves such a method out, or declares it at another
header, where each object defines it (row~841 of the revival's gap
ledger).
The compiled type checker compares a value parameter of an object
declaration by its modifiers other than \KWD{var}: it takes a component's
object declaration whose value parameter is declared \KWD{var} where the
exported one's is not, as \TYP{OneShot}'s parameter \VAR{canTryIt} in
\TYP{OneShotFlag}.
The rule above, like the matching definition of \secref{apis}, asks the same
header, and an object's header holds its value parameters with their
modifiers (row~844 of the revival's gap ledger).
The compiled type checker compares no name of a value parameter of an object
declaration: a component's object declaration whose value parameter is named
\VAR{z} satisfies an exported one whose value parameter is named \VAR{a}, so
that a compiled client that reads the field \VAR{a} stops at run time with
\texttt{NoSuchMethodError}, and one whose two value parameters have each
other's names satisfies the exported one too (row~839 of the revival's gap
ledger).
The compiled type checker takes only a field declaration as satisfying a field
declaration of an exported trait, where \secref{export-statements} takes a
getter declaration too: a component's trait that declares a getter \VAR{x} for
the exported trait's field \VAR{x} is refused (``different field'', row~842 of
the revival's gap ledger).
The compiled type checker takes only a method declaration with the same
header, its return type included, as satisfying a method declaration of an
exported trait that is not abstract, where \secref{export-statements} takes one
whose return type is a subtype of the exported one's: a component's method
\VAR{m} whose return type is \TYP{B}, where \TYP{B} extends \TYP{A}, does not
satisfy an exported method \VAR{m} whose return type is \TYP{A} (``different
method''); whether the rule or the check is to change is open (row~834 of the
revival's gap ledger).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/components/source-code.tex},
lines 380--385, which the change revises:
\begin{quote}
and contains,
for each field declaration and non-abstract method declaration
in the exported declaration,
a satisfying declaration (or a set of declarations).
When a trait has an abstract method declared,
a satisfying trait declaration is allowed to provide a concrete declaration.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

content.content:
== explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md:169-207

### 3.3 The covariance example, E1 (`basic/trait-parameters.tex`)

Original:

Base `Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-351`; the Working Draft of February 2011, `Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex:339-351` (the same text, compared by `git hash-object`):

```latex
Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of
themselves. For example, we can write:
%trait C[\S\] extends C[\T\]
%  where {S extends T, T extends Object}
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket \KWD{extends} C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{where} \{S \KWD{extends} T, T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Object}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
In this declaration, for every subtype \VAR{S} of \VAR{T}, \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket}
is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}. Effectively, we have expressed
  the fact that the static parameter \VAR{S} of \VAR{C} is covariant.
```

New text: `trait-parameters.tex:351-397`. The declaration kept, with "(* Not allowed! *)" added as the first line of its `%` source and of its typeset block, the typeset lines otherwise byte for byte; the sentence that it would express covariance and is not allowed; "Static parameters are invariant: C[\S\] is a subtype of C[\T\] only if S and T are the same type"; the widening function:

```
trait C[\S\]
  getter item(): S
end
object CItem[\S\](item: S) extends C[\S\] end
widen[\T, S extends T\](c: C[\S\]): C[\T\] = CItem[\T\](c.item)
```

and the callout, whose `covariant` sentence is: "The type group's later design declares variance instead with a covariant modifier on a static parameter (the team's later Types chapter, Luchangco, 2012), which is implemented on neither the interpreter nor the compiled path; the revival's decision record and row 404 of its gap ledger say what is known of it."

Reason: judgement section 3.1, E1, option 1; the library's widening functions (`Library/CovariantCollection.fss:15-36`, `upward[\R, I extends R, T extends R\]` and `opr APPCOV[\T, A extends T, B extends T\]`). The widening example as printed, completed into a program with a `Dog` and an `Animal`, prints `dog` under `walk` and compiled (`probes/examples/SpecWiden.fss`, `.walk.txt`, `.compile.txt`, `.run.txt`); the judgement's `AltCovariantBounded`, with `Any` bounds, does the same (`explorations/reviews/spec-refused-examples/captures/AltCovariantBounded.walk.txt`, `.run.txt`).

The `covariant` keyword, the type group's later direction. The later chapter's prose: "A static parameter of a trait declaration may be declared with the covariant modifier. In this case, it is a covariant parameter of the generic type defined by the trait declaration. One instantiation of a generic type is a subtype of another instantiation of the same generic type if the argument instantiating each covariant parameter in the first instantiation is a subtype of the corresponding argument in the second instantiation, and the argument instantiating each non-covariant parameter is the same in both instantiations." (`types.tick:322-339`, its comment lines left out); and its exclusion between instantiations: "Two instantiations of a generic trait type exclude each other if the corresponding arguments for any covariant parameter exclude each other, or if the corresponding arguments for any non-covariant parameter are not type equivalent." (`types.tick:357-360`). The keyword entered the grammar in `26718e298` (2011-12-06) and subtyping by variance in `20a8febe9` (2012-02-29) (ledger row 404). Today the compiled checker accepts it and the compiled run dies with `IncompatibleClassChangeError`, while `walk` refuses the binding (`explorations/reviews/spec-refused-examples/captures/AltCovariantVariance.compile.txt`, `.run.txt`, `.walk.txt`; row 404). It is the road by which declaration-site variance can return, once both paths carry it to run time (worklist item 12, `POSITIONS.md:131`); the text mentions it in one callout sentence and specifies nothing of it, since it runs on neither path.

Route C: the same under route C (section 3.2).

#!/bin/bash
# Compile-path ladder, restricted to the files this rung can affect.
#
# A copy of ../run-ladder.sh with two changes: the ladder root and output
# directory are private to this worktree, and the two whole-corpus loops are
# replaced by one driven by subset.txt (corpus<TAB>file per line).
#
# Pushes every interpreter test program (ProjectFortress/tests/*.fss) and every
# file in ProjectFortress/not_working_library_tests/ through the compiler path
# unchanged and records how far each one gets.
#
# Reproduce:  bash explorations/compile-ladder/run-ladder.sh
# Outputs:    explorations/compile-ladder/raw/<corpus>/<name>.{compile,run}
#             explorations/compile-ladder/results.tsv
#
# The run uses a private cache tree so it never touches default_repository/caches
# (fortress.caches system property + FORTRESS_CACHES env; ProjectProperties.java:283,
# same mechanism the suite uses at build.xml:941-943), and a private java.io.tmpdir
# so the 5.8 MB Rats! temp directory of every grammar-importing run (RatsUtil.java:138-144)
# is swept per file instead of filling the disk.

set -u

source "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/../../../explorations/experiment/env.sh"

LADDER_ROOT="${LADDER_ROOT:-$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp/ladder-r1}"
export LADDER_CACHES="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-caches"
export LADDER_TMP="$LADDER_ROOT/ladder-tmp"
export FORTRESS_CACHES="$LADDER_CACHES"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx2g -Xss64m -Dfortress.caches=$LADDER_CACHES -Djava.io.tmpdir=$LADDER_TMP"

PRISTINE="$LADDER_ROOT/pristine"
OUT="$FORTRESS_HOME/explorations/compile-ladder/repair-r1-atomic-static"
RAW="$OUT/raw"
TSV="$OUT/results.tsv"

COMPILE_TIMEOUT=120
RUN_TIMEOUT=60
MIN_FREE_KB=512000

mkdir -p "$RAW/tests" "$RAW/not_working_library_tests" "$LADDER_TMP"

disk_guard () {
    local free
    free=$(df -P / | awk 'NR==2{print $4}')
    if [ "$free" -lt "$MIN_FREE_KB" ]; then
        echo "STOP: only ${free} KB free on / (floor ${MIN_FREE_KB} KB)" | tee -a "$OUT/ladder.log"
        exit 2
    fi
    echo "-- disk free ${free} KB, cache $(du -sm "$LADDER_CACHES" | cut -f1) MB"
}

# Step 1: the compiler-world library, in the order repo-internals.md gives.
build_library () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    local f
    for f in LibraryBuiltin/AnyType.fss LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerLibrary.fss ../Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss \
             ../Library/CompilerSystem.fss ; do
        echo "library: $f"
        timeout 600 ../bin/fortress compile "$f" || { echo "LIBRARY BUILD FAILED on $f"; exit 1; }
    done
}

# Step 2: one known-good compiled program must print PASS before the ladder starts.
sanity () {
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1
    timeout 200 ../bin/fortress compile library_tests/Integer1.fss > /dev/null 2>&1 || return 1
    timeout 60 ../bin/fortress run Integer1 2>&1 | grep -q PASS
}

# Keep only the library's own cache entries; a program's entries are never reused.
prune_cache () {
    ( cd "$LADDER_CACHES" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.now"
    ( cd "$PRISTINE" && find . -type f -print ) | sort > "$LADDER_TMP/.keep"
    comm -23 "$LADDER_TMP/.now" "$LADDER_TMP/.keep" | while read -r p; do
        rm -f "$LADDER_CACHES/$p"
    done
}

component_of () {
    # component/api name as declared, which is what `fortress run` wants
    sed -n 's/^[[:space:]]*\(component\|api\)[[:space:]]\+\([A-Za-z0-9_.]\+\).*/\2/p' "$1" | head -1
}

run_one () {
    local corpus="$1" path="$2"
    local base name comp crc rrc t0 t1 ct rt
    base=$(basename "$path")
    name="${base%.*}"
    comp=$(component_of "$path")
    [ -n "$comp" ] || comp="$name"

    t0=$(date +%s)
    timeout -k 5 "$COMPILE_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress compile "$path" \
        > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.compile" 2>&1
    crc=$?
    t1=$(date +%s); ct=$((t1-t0))

    rrc=""
    rt=""
    if [ "$crc" -eq 0 ] && [ "${base##*.}" = "fss" ]; then
        t0=$(date +%s)
        timeout -k 5 "$RUN_TIMEOUT" ../bin/fortress run "$comp" \
            > "$RAW/$corpus/$base.run" 2>&1
        rrc=$?
        t1=$(date +%s); rt=$((t1-t0))
    fi

    printf '%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n' \
        "$corpus" "$base" "$comp" "$crc" "$rrc" "$ct" "$rt" >> "$TSV"
    echo "$corpus/$base crc=$crc rrc=$rrc ${ct}s"
}

main () {
    echo "=== ladder start $(date -Is) ==="
    disk_guard
    if [ ! -d "$PRISTINE" ]; then
        build_library
        rm -rf "$PRISTINE"; cp -a "$LADDER_CACHES" "$PRISTINE"
    fi
    sanity || { echo "SANITY FAILED: library_tests/Integer1 did not print PASS"; exit 1; }
    echo "sanity ok: library_tests/Integer1 compiles and prints PASS"
    prune_cache

    : > "$TSV"
    cd "$FORTRESS_HOME/ProjectFortress" || exit 1

    local n=0 line corpus f
    while IFS=$'\t' read -r corpus f; do
        [ -n "$corpus" ] || continue
        run_one "$corpus" "$corpus/$f"
        n=$((n+1))
        rm -rf "${LADDER_TMP:?}"/fortress*rats
        if [ $((n % 10)) -eq 0 ]; then prune_cache; disk_guard; fi
    done < "$OUT/subset.txt"
    prune_cache
    echo "=== ladder done $(date -Is), $n files ==="
    disk_guard
}

main "$@"

FortressBuiltin

api FortressBuiltin
The builtinPrimitive function is actually recognized as a special piece of built-in
magic by the Fortress interpreter and, where its argument names a helper, by the
compiler. The javaClass argument names either a glue class, a Java Class which is
a subclass of com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.NativeApp, which provides code for
the closure which is used in place of the call to builtinPrimitive and which only the
interpreter runs, or a helper, a public static method of a Java class of the package
com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers, written com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method,
which both the interpreter and the compiled code call. The interpreter loads a
helper beside its glue classes: among the methods of that name it takes the one
whose Java parameter and result types carry the declared types, self first, and
it carries each value at its declared type. The compiler, before type checking,
rewrites the body into a call of the helper, which the type checker checks against
the helper’s Java signature. A string under com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers that
names no such method is an error on both. Meanwhile all the necessary type information,
argument names, etc. must be declared here in Fortress-land. For examples, see
the end of this file.
R E V I S E D B Y T H E 2026 R E V I V A L

SEE

Section I.1.44

The argument names a static helper of com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers, which both the
interpreter and the compiled code call, as well as a glue class, which only the interpreter
runs; the package of the glue classes is named as it is.

In practice, if you are extending the interpreter you will probably want to extend
com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.NativeFn0,1,2,3,4 or one of their subclasses defined
in com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim. These types are generally easier to
work with, and the boilerplate packing and unpacking of values is done for you.

<!-- The decision record of the revision of builtinPrimitive's printed comment (Appendix I, "A native binding that names a static helper"): the passage, the original and the new text, the reason, and the way back. -->

# Decision record: builtinPrimitive's comment names a static helper

## 1. The passage

`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:14-29`, the comment of `builtinPrimitive[\T\](javaClass:String):T` (`:30`). The specification prints it: `Specification/library/default-libraries.tex:37-39` inputs `library/apis/FortressBuiltin.tex`, which the specification's build typesets from the `.fsi` (`Specification/fortress/build.xml:129-139`, the `fortex` task over `${library.builtin.home}`). The Working Draft of February 2011 holds no copy of the comment: `Specification-1.0-frozen/library/default-libraries.tex:39` inputs the same generated file, which neither tree tracks (`git ls-files Specification-1.0-frozen/library/apis Specification/library/apis` prints nothing). So the original is quoted from the `.fsi` at the base, `3cd653815`, whose lines 14-29 equal those of the team's last commit, `a874948ac` (compared with `cmp`).

## 2. The original

```
(** The %builtinPrimitive% function is actually recognized as a special piece
    of built-in magic by the Fortress interpreter.  The %javaClass%
    argument names a Java Class which is a subclass of
    \texttt{com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.NativeApp}, which provides code
    for the closure which is used in place of the call to
    %builtinPrimitive%.  Meanwhile all the necessary type information,
    argument names, etc. must be declared here in Fortress-land.  For
    examples, see the end of this file.

    In practice, if you are extending the interpreter you will probably
    want to extend \texttt{com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.NativeFn0,1,2,3,4}
    or one of their subclasses defined in
    \texttt{com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.primitive}.  These types are
    generally easier to work with, and the boilerplate packing and
    unpacking of values is done for you.
**)
```

## 3. The new text

The same sixteen lines, so that no later line of the api moves (354 citations of `FortressBuiltin.fsi:<line>` under `explorations/` name lines below it):

- The first sentence: recognized "by the Fortress interpreter and, where its argument names a helper, by the compiler".
- The argument "names either a glue class, a Java Class which is a subclass of `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.NativeApp`, which provides code for the closure ... and which only the interpreter runs, or a helper, a public static method of a Java class of the package `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers`, written `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.`*Class*`.`*method*, which both the interpreter and the compiled code call."
- "The interpreter loads a helper beside its glue classes: among the methods of that name it takes the one whose Java parameter and result types carry the declared types, `self` first, and it carries each value at its declared type. The compiler, before type checking, rewrites the body into a call of the helper, which the type checker checks against the helper's Java signature. A string under `com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers` that names no such method is an error on both."
- The callout `\revision{revival-native-helpers}{...}` after the first paragraph: "The argument names a glue class, which only the interpreter runs, or a static helper of com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers, which both the interpreter and the compiled code call; and the package that defines the subclasses of the NativeFn classes is named as the implementation names it." The api's typesetting carries it: the built PDF prints the box under the first paragraph, "REVISED BY THE 2026 REVIVAL SEE Section I.1.44" (`pdftotext` of `Specification/fortress/fortress.pdf`).
- The second paragraph: `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.primitive` becomes `com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim`, the package that holds the subclasses of `NativeFn0` to `NativeFn4` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/`; `interpreter/glue/` has no `primitive/`, and `git log --all -- 'ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/primitive/*'` prints nothing). Otherwise unchanged.

## 4. The reason

The curator's decision of 10 October 2026 (P-58): every native binding of the one library keeps the library's own form, a body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, and its string names a static helper of `nativeHelpers/` in place of a glue class, which the compiled path cannot use, since a glue class takes walk's boxed values (`interpreter/glue/prim/Util.java:253-254`, `SS2B.applyToArgs(FValue x, FValue y)`), where the compiled path calls static helpers over plain Java values. Walk loads the helper through a loader beside its glue classes (this rung, `interpreter/glue/StaticNativeApp.java`, hooked in `NativeApp.checkAndLoadNative`), and the compiled path rewrites each such body at the parse into a call (the batch's other half). Twenty-one bindings now name helpers (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:741-810`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss:371`, `:373`), so the comment's "names a Java Class which is a subclass of ... NativeApp" no longer covers every binding. The second paragraph's package name was already false; it is corrected in the same revision because the comment is revised whole and the revision vouches for it.

The sentences of the comment that the batch's tests show:
- walk loads a helper and carries values at the declared types: `ProjectFortress/tests/NativeHelperBindingWalk.fss`, the family `NativeHelperFamilyZZ32Walk.fss`;
- walk takes the overload by the declared types: `NativeHelperBindingWalk.fss`, `bazS` and `bazI` over `simpleOverload.baz`;
- a string under the package that names no such method is refused at load: `NativeHelperMisspeltWalk.fss` with its `.test`; no overload that fits, `NativeHelperMisfitWalk`; a declared type that no Java type carries, `NativeHelperUncarriedWalk`;
- the compiled half's rewrite and refusal: the other half's compiled tests.

## 5. The way back

Restore the sixteen lines of section 2, put the 21 strings back on their glue classes (`Int$Eq` to `ZZ32$ToNN32`, `Int$ToString`), drop the loader's hook, and the compiled path again has no binding of the one library's natives that it can call (row 309). The alternative not taken in P-58, `import java` declarations written in the library, would need the comment to say that the library also binds natives that way, and walk's `import java` path, which five gaps stop (F-180).
EOF
echo written

#!/bin/bash
# The gate's checker-count stage: run the bytecode compiler's static checker over the
# INTERPRETER's library, with the interpreter's prelude in scope, and print the per-api
# error table, the total and the crash line that follows it.
#
# Why it exists: POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-21, "the library route" - one library, the
# interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks - and step 1 of
# coordinator/library-route-judgement.md, which makes the distance to that goal a
# permanent gate stage rather than a one-off script. A change in the count is reported, not red (checker-gate-review.md).
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched:
# javac output and the checker's caches go to the scratch directory (default: $TMPDIR
# or /tmp), and the caches are given to the JVM as -Dfortress.caches, honoured through
# ProjectProperties.java:261-269,283, so default_repository/ is never read or written.
# Exit 0 if the table holds a total; 1 if no table could be produced, or if the table holds
# no total because the run's errors are not the checker's (#stopped, below). 20 s in the
# main tree, measured 2026-09-22; it needs no library rebuild and no warm cache.
#
# The run stops after the type checker (WorldFlip -stop check), since 2026-10-24 (climb batch
# 22): the compiler's own phase order up to and including TYPECHECK, integer literal folding
# included, as the distance stage's DistanceMulti -order check. Past the checker, the code
# generator's refusals are not the checker's errors (FACTS F-34 counts them), and its first
# one throws, so a run on a library the checker passes went on into the code generator and
# printed no total. A run the checker stops runs the same phases as before; a clean check,
# a run that reached the component's check and ended rc 0 with no error line, reads as 0.
#
#!/bin/bash
# The gate's distance stage: the compiled checker over the whole interpreter library, the
# fourteen components, the prelude's twelve and the two that List imports, and their apis,
# every stage of every unit run whatever the earlier stages reported, so that nothing hides
# behind an early return; one table.
#
# Why it exists: Pavol's answer 11 (POSITIONS.md, 2026-09-26): the full measurement of the
# distance to the switch-over "becomes a report-only stage of phase 3's gates, whose job is
# driving it down". The checker-count stage beside it (../checker-count/run.sh) sees only
# the errors before each api's early return, 62 of about 1,740 on 2026-09-27.
#
# Run from $FORTRESS_HOME with explorations/experiment/env.sh sourced, after ant compileAll:
#
#     explorations/coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh <out-file> [scratch-dir] [setting]
#
# It writes the table to <out-file> and prints it. Nothing in the tree is touched: the
# shadow sources and classes, the driver, the checker's caches (-Dfortress.caches) and the
# JVM's temporary directory (so Rats! leaves nothing in /tmp) go to the scratch directory
# (default: $TMPDIR or /tmp), and the caches are deleted at the end. It never removes
# /tmp/fortress*rats, which other runs on the machine use. Exit 0 if the table was
# produced, 1 if it could not be. One JVM, -Xmx4g, one busy core: 789 s on the idle 4-CPU
# container on 2026-09-27, 14 to 24 minutes under load 7 to 18 (switch-over-distance-flat.md
# section 5); the table's #seconds and #machine rows say what each run took and where.
#
# The setting: "compile" by default, the compile command's own: DistanceMulti's -setting
# compile takes the extends-Object pre-desugaring from the line that opens
# Shell.useCompilerLibraries() in the tracked ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/Shell.java,
# read at each run (the run stops, with no total, if that line is not there; its "### order="
# line prints the switch it read, extendsObject=...), and turns the compiled-expression
